title: Step‑by‑Step Guide to Thin‑Sliced Kohlrabi for Crunchy Slaws
meta_description: Learn how to thin slice kohlrabi with a mandoline for crisp slaws. Follow our step‑by‑step guide, safety tips, and seasoning ideas for perfect texture.
html:
Thinly sliced kohlrabi makes a surprisingly crunchy addition to any slaw, and the secret to getting those restaurant‑thin ribbons quickly is a good mandoline. In this guide we’ll walk through selecting a kohlrabi, prepping it, and using a thin sliced kohlrabi mandoline to achieve uniform slices that hold up in dressings and stay crisp.

Choosing the Right Kohlrabi

Start with fresh kohlrabi that feels firm and heavy for its size. Look for a smooth, unblemished skin—green or purple varieties both work. Smaller bulbs are naturally sweeter, while larger ones have a milder, more earthy flavor. Trim the leaves (you can save them for a sauté) and give the bulb a quick rinse.

Preparing Your Workspace and Safety Gear

Before you reach for the mandoline, set up a safe cutting station. Place a damp kitchen towel under your cutting board to prevent slipping. Most mandolines, including the Mandoline Slicer, come with a hand guard; always use it. If you’re new to mandoline work, consider a cut‑resistant glove on your free hand.

Using a Thin Sliced Kohlrabi Mandoline

The Mandoline Slicer offers adjustable thickness settings, which is perfect for slaw because you can dial in a 1‑2 mm slice for that delicate bite. Here’s how to get consistent results:

  1. Set the blade to the thinnest setting (usually marked “1”).
  2. Secure the kohlrabi in the hand guard, stem side down.
  3. Slide the guard back and forth across the blade in a smooth, steady motion. Let the mandoline do the work; don’t force the vegetable.
  4. Collect the ribbons in a bowl as you go, shaking the mandoline gently to release any that cling to the blade.

If you need a slightly thicker texture for heartier slaws, adjust the blade to the next setting and repeat. The key is uniformity—every ribbon should be the same thickness, which ensures even dressing absorption.

Seasoning and Assembling the Slaw

Once you have a pile of thin sliced kohlrabi, it’s ready for the mix‑in stage. Because the slices are so fine, they absorb flavors quickly. A classic vinaigrette of apple cider vinegar, a touch of honey, Dijon mustard, and olive oil works beautifully. Toss the ribbons with a pinch of salt, then drizzle the dressing and give the slaw a gentle toss. Add complementary crunch like shredded carrots, thin sliced radish, or toasted sesame seeds for extra texture.

Cleaning and Maintaining Your Mandoline

After you’ve sliced, the Mandoline Slicer is easy to clean. Most models are dishwasher‑safe, but a quick hand wash with warm, soapy water prolongs the blade’s sharpness. Use a soft brush to dislodge any vegetable fibers stuck in the blade slots. Never submerge the whole unit if the handle is wooden; instead, wipe the handle dry.

Tips for Perfectly Crunchy Kohlrabi Slaw

  • Ice water soak: For an extra crisp bite, submerge the sliced kohlrabi in ice water for 5‑10 minutes, then drain well before dressing.
  • Dry before dressing: Pat the slices dry with a clean kitchen towel to prevent excess moisture diluting your vinaigrette.
  • Batch slice: If you’re preparing a large slaw, slice all the kohlrabi first, then store the ribbons in a sealed container in the fridge for up to 24 hours.

With these steps, you can turn a humble root vegetable into a star side dish that’s both elegant and budget‑friendly.

FAQ

Do I need a special blade for kohlrabi?

No. The standard straight blade on the Mandoline Slicer handles kohlrabi just fine. If you prefer a wavy texture, many mandolines include interchangeable blades, but the straight blade gives the cleanest, restaurant‑thin slices.

Can I use the mandoline for other vegetables in slaw?

Absolutely. Thin sliced carrots, daikon radish, and even apples respond well to the same technique. Just adjust the thickness setting to match the desired crunch level.

Is the hand guard enough protection for my fingers?

The hand guard is designed to keep your fingers away from the blade, but a cut‑resistant glove adds an extra layer of safety, especially if you’re new to mandoline slicing.
